\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

The probe reward trap reveals that behavioral death can precede distributional collapse by 1{,}300 steps, evading entropy monitoring entirely.

Practitioners should verify geometric separability before deploying concept directions as rewards, and complement entropy monitoring with behavioral metrics that directly measure the target capability.

\section{When Does Discriminability Fail as Reward Utility?}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Root cause of the probe reward trap.}
The probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) and the cosine failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) share a common geometric root.
$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
Although $\dsyc$ separability correlates with evidence strength (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}), it encodes \emph{how much} belief changed, not whether the change was appropriate (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation generalizes: Llama-3-8B achieves comparable discriminability (AUROC $0.779$) yet the semantic gap persists.
This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve.
\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} reinforce this principle: concept directions succeed when shortcut behaviors are geometrically separable.
Independent work corroborates the limitation: persona vectors are geometrically independent of $\dsyc$ \citep{kelkar2026persona}, and sycophancy decomposes into independently steerable sub-behaviors \citep{vennemeyer2025sycophancy} that $\dsyc$ projects onto a single axis.

\paragraph{GRPO results under our configuration.}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Comparison of all sycophancy calibration methods on Qwen3-8B. $\sycon$ is the harmonic mean of the true-positive flip rate ($\tof$) and no-flip rate ($\nof$); higher indicates better calibration. Best result in \textbf{bold}. $^\dagger$Best checkpoint (seed 1, step 6500); only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla. $^\ddagger$Seed 2 (15 checkpoints); all exceed vanilla. Best $\sycon{=}0.286$ (step 7000). $^\S$All cosine variants collapsed from step 1 ($\tof{=}0$ at every checkpoint); F1d additionally diverged at step 2160 (entropy ${<}\,0.01$). $^\P$ACT and ActAdd differ from GRPO along 5+ dimensions (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); included for context, not as controlled comparisons. }
\label{tab:main_comparison}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}
\toprule
Method & Type & $\sycon$ $\uparrow$ & $\tof$ $\uparrow$ & $\nof$ $\uparrow$ & Step \\
\midrule
Vanilla & -- & 0.134 & 0.072 & 0.945 & -- \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO with $\dsyc$}} \\
Cosine $\rone$ (F1a--F1d) & RL & 0.000$^\S$ & 0.000 & 1.000 & 500 \\
Binary Probe $\rone$ (F2) & RL & 0.000 & 0.000 & 0.995 & 500 \\
Continuous Probe $\rone$ (F3) & RL & 0.124 & 0.066 & 0.934 & 500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO without $\dsyc$}} \\
$\rthree$-only GRPO & RL & 0.153$^\dagger$ & 0.083 & 0.983 & 6500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{Reference methods (not directly comparable)$^\P$}} \\
ActAdd ($\alpha{=}5$) & Inference & 0.054 & 0.028 & 0.961 & -- \\
\textbf{ACT} (seed 1) & SFT & \textbf{0.301} & \textbf{0.182} & 0.867 & 8000 \\
ACT (seed 2)$^\ddagger$ & SFT & 0.286 & 0.171 & 0.862 & 7000 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

If the cosine and probe failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}--\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) were caused by $\dsyc$ alone, removing it should recover calibration.
$\rthree$-only GRPO tests this hypothesis by relying solely on the NLI behavioral reward, and fails: only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla (14.3\%; gs$=$2 only, gs$=$8 ablation reported separately), with both seeds oscillating ($\Delta \approx 0.069$) before diverging (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}; Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}).
The failure is not representational: $\dsyc$ AUROC varies by ${<}0.01$ across checkpoints and $\rthree$ saturates at ${\sim}0.98$ ($p{=}0.703$), yet $\sycon$ swings by 17\%.
This disconnect between stable representations and unstable behavior points to the per-completion reward structure, not the reward content, as the bottleneck.

\paragraph{Competing hypotheses and ablation.}
Three explanations are consistent with these failures: (a)~$\dsyc$ is fundamentally unsuitable as a sycophancy reward; (b)~group size$=$2 provides insufficient ranking diversity; (c)~sycophancy calibration resists scalar per-completion RL.
We designed two ablations to discriminate among them (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}).
\emph{Group-size ablation.}
Per-completion GRPO fails at both group sizes 2 and 8; gs$=$8 also fails (all below vanilla; terminated early), ruling out insufficient ranking diversity.
\emph{LoRA-controlled comparison.}
Reducing ACT to GRPO's LoRA configuration (rank 64, $\alpha{=}64$, 4 modules) still yields $\sycon = 0.267$ (peak 0.326), with all 16 checkpoints exceeding vanilla.
Under identical adapters, per-token SFT achieves $1.7{\times}$ higher $\sycon$ ($0.267$ vs.\ $0.153$), identifying supervision granularity as one plausible explanation, independently corroborated by SMART's per-step success~\citep{beigi2025smart}; confounds are discussed in Limitations.
The probe reward trap provides independent evidence for~(a): the trap arises despite the probe being non-differentiable, ruling out gradient-based exploitation as the mechanism.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Ablation: isolating supervision paradigm from LoRA configuration. All methods use Qwen3-8B with $\rthree$ (behavioral reward). Vanilla $\sycon{=}0.134$. $^\dagger$Terminated early after three checkpoints showed declining trajectory. $^\ddagger$Peak at step 7000; final checkpoint (step 8000) $\sycon{=}0.267$.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcc@{}}
\toprule
Method & LoRA config & Best $\sycon$ & ${>}$Van. \\
\midrule
GRPO gs$=$2 (2 seeds) & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.153 & 4/28 \\
GRPO gs$=$8$^\dagger$ & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.085 & 0/3 \\
\midrule
ACT reduced-LoRA$^\ddagger$ & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.326 & 16/16 \\
ACT full s1 & r64, $\alpha$128, 7m & 0.301 & 16/16 \\
ACT full s2 & r64, $\alpha$128, 7m & 0.286 & 15/15 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_trajectory.pdf}
\caption{$\sycon$ trajectories for $\rthree$-only GRPO (two seeds) and ACT (two seeds) over training steps. ACT exceeds vanilla at every evaluated checkpoint (31/31 across two seeds); $\rthree$-only GRPO exceeds vanilla at only 4/28 checkpoints (14.3\%).}
\label{fig:trajectory}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{ACT vs.\ GRPO.}
ACT's advantage is not marginal but categorical: its worst checkpoint ($\sycon{=}0.170$) exceeds GRPO's absolute best ($\sycon{=}0.153$), and both seeds maintain above-vanilla performance throughout training (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}; held-out evaluation confirms generalization: ACT $\sycon{=}0.205$, $3.7{\times}$ vanilla, vs.\ $\rthree$-only GRPO $0.108$, $1.9{\times}$; see Limitations).
The reduced-LoRA ablation (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}) confirms this is not an adapter-capacity artifact, leaving supervision granularity as one plausible explanatory variable.

\paragraph{Relationship to inference-time probe methods.}
\citet{papadatos2024probepenalties} reduce sycophancy using a probe of comparable quality (94\% accuracy) via Best-of-N reranking without producing gradients.
This suggests two orthogonal failure dimensions: (1)~inside vs.\ outside the optimization loop, where reward optimization enables the probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}), while inference-time reranking sidesteps it; and (2)~scalar per-completion reward, where the failure persists even without the probe ($\rthree$-only GRPO).

\paragraph{Future directions.}
Per-step process rewards offer the most direct path forward: SMART~\citep{beigi2025smart} succeeds at sycophancy calibration by detecting premature concession at individual reasoning steps---a temporal signature that bypasses $\dsyc$'s geometric inseparability and that scalar per-completion rewards compress away.
Whether attributes with similar geometric entanglement~\citep{skalse2022hacking} exhibit the same failures remains open.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Representation Engineering.}
Linear directions in LLM residual streams encode behavioral concepts \citep{zou2023repe, marks2024geometry}; inference-time methods such as Inference-Time Intervention \citep[ITI;][]{li2023iti}, Activation Addition \citep[ActAdd;][]{turner2023actadd}, and Contrastive Activation Addition \citep[CAA;][]{rimsky2024caa} demonstrate that activation geometry suffices for behavioral control \citep{burns2023ccs}, but we find that $\dsyc$ fails when used as an RL reward despite succeeding at inference time.

\paragraph{Reward Design and Overoptimization.}
Proxy rewards diverge from true objectives under sustained optimization \citep{gao2023scaling, pan2022effects}.
\citet{manheim2019goodhart} taxonomize four Goodhart variants: \emph{regressional} (proxy-target correlation breaks under optimization shift), \emph{extremal} (divergence at distribution tails), \emph{causal} (intervening on proxy severs its link to the target), and \emph{adversarial} (an agent explicitly exploits the proxy).
Our probe reward trap instantiates the regressional variant: $\dsyc$ discriminates sycophantic activations under the pre-training distribution but ceases to correlate with the target once optimization shifts the policy.
The failure is not extremal (collapse occurs at moderate optimization pressure, not distribution tails), not causal (stopped gradients prevent intervention on the direction), and not adversarial (the policy does not model the probe).
The incremental contribution over prior regressional analyses~\citep{gao2023scaling} is temporal: we document behavioral death within 500 steps---an order of magnitude faster than gradual degradation curves---and a 1{,}300-step lag that renders entropy monitoring blind~\citep{skalse2022hacking}.
\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} show that representation-level directions succeed when behaviors are geometrically separable (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\paragraph{Sycophancy Characterization and Mitigation.}
Sycophancy is pervasive in assistants trained via RLHF \citep{ouyang2022instructgpt, bai2022training, sharma2023sycophancy, perez2023discovering, shapira2026amplifies} and traceable to late-layer preference shifts \citep{wang2025internal}; it undermines broader truthfulness objectives \citep{lin2022truthfulqa} even when models possess the knowledge to respond accurately \citep{kadavath2022language}.
Mitigations span synthetic data \citep{wei2024synthetic}, consistency training \citep{consistency2025bctact}, and neuron-level correction \citep{obrien2025fewbadneurons}.
\citet{vennemeyer2025sycophancy} show that sycophancy decomposes into independently steerable sub-behaviors; a single $\dsyc$ captures only their shared variance, which is why the step from diagnosis to reward is structurally blocked.

\paragraph{Probe-Based and Representation-Guided Methods.}
Linear probing methodology is well-established for interpreting neural representations \citep{hewitt2019designing, belinkov2022probing}.
\citet{papadatos2024probepenalties} reduce sycophancy via Best-of-N reranking with linear probe penalties (94\% accuracy) without producing gradients; our work reveals what happens when a comparable signal enters the training loop (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Representation-guided RL has been extended to reasoning and gradient regularization \citep{zhang2026latentgrpo, luo2026craft, sinii2025smallvectors, ackermann2026gradreg}.
SMART \citep{beigi2025smart} applies per-step process rewards for sycophancy, succeeding where our completion-level rewards fail, consistent with ACT's per-token success and with broader evidence that process supervision outperforms outcome supervision \citep{lightman2024verify, uesato2022solving}.

\section{When Does Discriminability Fail as Reward Utility?}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Root cause of the probe reward trap.}
The probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) and the cosine failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) share a common geometric root.
$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
Although $\dsyc$ separability correlates with evidence strength (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}), it encodes \emph{how much} belief changed, not whether the change was appropriate (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation generalizes: Llama-3-8B achieves comparable discriminability (AUROC $0.779$) yet the semantic gap persists.
This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve.
\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} reinforce this principle: concept directions succeed when shortcut behaviors are geometrically separable.
Independent work corroborates the limitation: persona vectors are geometrically independent of $\dsyc$ \citep{kelkar2026persona}, and sycophancy decomposes into independently steerable sub-behaviors \citep{vennemeyer2025sycophancy} that $\dsyc$ projects onto a single axis.

\paragraph{GRPO results under our configuration.}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Comparison of all sycophancy calibration methods on Qwen3-8B. $\sycon$ is the harmonic mean of the true-positive flip rate ($\tof$) and no-flip rate ($\nof$); higher indicates better calibration. Best result in \textbf{bold}. $^\dagger$Best checkpoint (seed 1, step 6500); only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla. $^\ddagger$Seed 2 (15 checkpoints); all exceed vanilla. Best $\sycon{=}0.286$ (step 7000). $^\S$All cosine variants collapsed from step 1 ($\tof{=}0$ at every checkpoint); F1d additionally diverged at step 2160 (entropy ${<}\,0.01$). $^\P$ACT and ActAdd differ from GRPO along 5+ dimensions (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); included for context, not as controlled comparisons. }
\label{tab:main_comparison}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}
\toprule
Method & Type & $\sycon$ $\uparrow$ & $\tof$ $\uparrow$ & $\nof$ $\uparrow$ & Step \\
\midrule
Vanilla & -- & 0.134 & 0.072 & 0.945 & -- \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO with $\dsyc$}} \\
Cosine $\rone$ (F1a--F1d) & RL & 0.000$^\S$ & 0.000 & 1.000 & 500 \\
Binary Probe $\rone$ (F2) & RL & 0.000 & 0.000 & 0.995 & 500 \\
Continuous Probe $\rone$ (F3) & RL & 0.124 & 0.066 & 0.934 & 500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO without $\dsyc$}} \\
$\rthree$-only GRPO & RL & 0.153$^\dagger$ & 0.083 & 0.983 & 6500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{Reference methods (not directly comparable)$^\P$}} \\
ActAdd ($\alpha{=}5$) & Inference & 0.054 & 0.028 & 0.961 & -- \\
\textbf{ACT} (seed 1) & SFT & \textbf{0.301} & \textbf{0.182} & 0.867 & 8000 \\
ACT (seed 2)$^\ddagger$ & SFT & 0.286 & 0.171 & 0.862 & 7000 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

If the cosine and probe failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}--\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) were caused by $\dsyc$ alone, removing it should recover calibration.
$\rthree$-only GRPO tests this hypothesis by relying solely on the NLI behavioral reward, and fails: only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla (14.3\%; gs$=$2 only, gs$=$8 ablation reported separately), with both seeds oscillating ($\Delta \approx 0.069$) before diverging (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}; Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}).
The failure is not representational: $\dsyc$ AUROC varies by ${<}0.01$ across checkpoints and $\rthree$ saturates at ${\sim}0.98$ ($p{=}0.703$), yet $\sycon$ swings by 17\%.
This disconnect between stable representations and unstable behavior points to the per-completion reward structure, not the reward content, as the bottleneck.

\paragraph{Competing hypotheses and ablation.}
Three explanations are consistent with these failures: (a)~$\dsyc$ is fundamentally unsuitable as a sycophancy reward; (b)~group size$=$2 provides insufficient ranking diversity; (c)~sycophancy calibration resists scalar per-completion RL.
We designed two ablations to discriminate among them (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}).
\emph{Group-size ablation.}
Per-completion GRPO fails at both group sizes 2 and 8; gs$=$8 also fails (all below vanilla; terminated early), ruling out insufficient ranking diversity.
\emph{LoRA-controlled comparison.}
Reducing ACT to GRPO's LoRA configuration (rank 64, $\alpha{=}64$, 4 modules) still yields $\sycon = 0.267$ (peak 0.326), with all 16 checkpoints exceeding vanilla.
Under identical adapters, per-token SFT achieves $1.7{\times}$ higher $\sycon$ ($0.267$ vs.\ $0.153$), identifying supervision granularity as one plausible explanation, independently corroborated by SMART's per-step success~\citep{beigi2025smart}; confounds are discussed in Limitations.
The probe reward trap provides independent evidence for~(a): the trap arises despite the probe being non-differentiable, ruling out gradient-based exploitation as the mechanism.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Ablation: isolating supervision paradigm from LoRA configuration. All methods use Qwen3-8B with $\rthree$ (behavioral reward). Vanilla $\sycon{=}0.134$. $^\dagger$Terminated early after three checkpoints showed declining trajectory. $^\ddagger$Peak at step 7000; final checkpoint (step 8000) $\sycon{=}0.267$.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcc@{}}
\toprule
Method & LoRA config & Best $\sycon$ & ${>}$Van. \\
\midrule
GRPO gs$=$2 (2 seeds) & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.153 & 4/28 \\
GRPO gs$=$8$^\dagger$ & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.085 & 0/3 \\
\midrule
ACT reduced-LoRA$^\ddagger$ & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.326 & 16/16 \\
ACT full s1 & r64, $\alpha$128, 7m & 0.301 & 16/16 \\
ACT full s2 & r64, $\alpha$128, 7m & 0.286 & 15/15 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_trajectory.pdf}
\caption{$\sycon$ trajectories for $\rthree$-only GRPO (two seeds) and ACT (two seeds) over training steps. ACT exceeds vanilla at every evaluated checkpoint (31/31 across two seeds); $\rthree$-only GRPO exceeds vanilla at only 4/28 checkpoints (14.3\%).}
\label{fig:trajectory}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{ACT vs.\ GRPO.}
ACT's advantage is not marginal but categorical: its worst checkpoint ($\sycon{=}0.170$) exceeds GRPO's absolute best ($\sycon{=}0.153$), and both seeds maintain above-vanilla performance throughout training (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}; held-out evaluation confirms generalization: ACT $\sycon{=}0.205$, $3.7{\times}$ vanilla, vs.\ $\rthree$-only GRPO $0.108$, $1.9{\times}$; see Limitations).
The reduced-LoRA ablation (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}) confirms this is not an adapter-capacity artifact, leaving supervision granularity as one plausible explanatory variable.

\paragraph{Relationship to inference-time probe methods.}
\citet{papadatos2024probepenalties} reduce sycophancy via Best-of-N reranking with a probe of comparable quality (94\% accuracy) without producing gradients, suggesting two orthogonal failure dimensions: (1)~inside vs.\ outside the optimization loop, and (2)~scalar per-completion reward, where the failure persists even without the probe ($\rthree$-only GRPO).

\paragraph{Future directions.}
Per-step process rewards offer the most direct path forward: SMART~\citep{beigi2025smart} succeeds at sycophancy calibration by detecting premature concession at individual reasoning steps---a temporal signature that bypasses $\dsyc$'s geometric inseparability and that scalar per-completion rewards compress away.
Whether attributes with similar geometric entanglement~\citep{skalse2022hacking} exhibit the same failures remains open.

\section{When Does Discriminability Fail as Reward Utility?}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Root cause of the probe reward trap.}
The probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) and the cosine failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) share a common geometric root.
$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
Although $\dsyc$ separability correlates with evidence strength (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}), it encodes \emph{how much} belief changed, not whether the change was appropriate (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation generalizes: Llama-3-8B achieves comparable discriminability (AUROC $0.779$) yet the semantic gap persists.
This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve.
\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} reinforce this principle: concept directions succeed when shortcut behaviors are geometrically separable.
Independent work corroborates the limitation: persona vectors are geometrically independent of $\dsyc$ \citep{kelkar2026persona}, and sycophancy decomposes into independently steerable sub-behaviors \citep{vennemeyer2025sycophancy} that $\dsyc$ projects onto a single axis.

\paragraph{GRPO results under our configuration.}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Comparison of all sycophancy calibration methods on Qwen3-8B. $\sycon$ is the harmonic mean of the true-positive flip rate ($\tof$) and no-flip rate ($\nof$); higher indicates better calibration. Best result in \textbf{bold}. $^\dagger$Best checkpoint (seed 1, step 6500); only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla. $^\ddagger$Seed 2 (15 checkpoints); all exceed vanilla. Best $\sycon{=}0.286$ (step 7000). $^\S$All cosine variants collapsed from step 1 ($\tof{=}0$ at every checkpoint); F1d additionally diverged at step 2160 (entropy ${<}\,0.01$). $^\P$ACT and ActAdd differ from GRPO along 5+ dimensions (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); included for context, not as controlled comparisons. }
\label{tab:main_comparison}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}
\toprule
Method & Type & $\sycon$ $\uparrow$ & $\tof$ $\uparrow$ & $\nof$ $\uparrow$ & Step \\
\midrule
Vanilla & -- & 0.134 & 0.072 & 0.945 & -- \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO with $\dsyc$}} \\
Cosine $\rone$ (F1a--F1d) & RL & 0.000$^\S$ & 0.000 & 1.000 & 500 \\
Binary Probe $\rone$ (F2) & RL & 0.000 & 0.000 & 0.995 & 500 \\
Continuous Probe $\rone$ (F3) & RL & 0.124 & 0.066 & 0.934 & 500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO without $\dsyc$}} \\
$\rthree$-only GRPO & RL & 0.153$^\dagger$ & 0.083 & 0.983 & 6500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{Reference methods (not directly comparable)$^\P$}} \\
ActAdd ($\alpha{=}5$) & Inference & 0.054 & 0.028 & 0.961 & -- \\
\textbf{ACT} (seed 1) & SFT & \textbf{0.301} & \textbf{0.182} & 0.867 & 8000 \\
ACT (seed 2)$^\ddagger$ & SFT & 0.286 & 0.171 & 0.862 & 7000 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

If the cosine and probe failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}--\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) were caused by $\dsyc$ alone, removing it should recover calibration.
$\rthree$-only GRPO tests this hypothesis by relying solely on the NLI behavioral reward, and fails: only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla (14.3\%; gs$=$2 only, gs$=$8 ablation reported separately), with both seeds oscillating ($\Delta \approx 0.069$) before diverging (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}; Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}).
The failure is not representational: $\dsyc$ AUROC varies by ${<}0.01$ across checkpoints and $\rthree$ saturates at ${\sim}0.98$ ($p{=}0.703$), yet $\sycon$ swings by 17\%.
This disconnect between stable representations and unstable behavior points to the per-completion reward structure, not the reward content, as the bottleneck.

\paragraph{Competing hypotheses and ablation.}
Three explanations are consistent with these failures: (a)~$\dsyc$ is fundamentally unsuitable as a sycophancy reward; (b)~group size$=$2 provides insufficient ranking diversity; (c)~sycophancy calibration resists scalar per-completion RL.
Two ablations discriminate among them (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}).
GRPO fails at both group sizes 2 and 8 (gs$=$8 terminated early, all below vanilla), ruling out~(b).
Reducing ACT to GRPO's LoRA configuration (rank 64, $\alpha{=}64$, 4 modules) still yields $\sycon = 0.267$ (peak 0.326), with all 16 checkpoints exceeding vanilla; under matched adapters, per-token SFT achieves $1.7{\times}$ higher $\sycon$ ($0.267$ vs.\ $0.153$), identifying supervision granularity as one plausible explanation~\citep{beigi2025smart}; confounds are discussed in Limitations.
The probe reward trap independently supports~(a): the trap arises despite stopped gradients, ruling out gradient-based exploitation.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Ablation: isolating supervision paradigm from LoRA configuration. All methods use Qwen3-8B with $\rthree$ (behavioral reward). Vanilla $\sycon{=}0.134$. $^\dagger$Terminated early after three checkpoints showed declining trajectory. $^\ddagger$Peak at step 7000; final checkpoint (step 8000) $\sycon{=}0.267$.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcc@{}}
\toprule
Method & LoRA config & Best $\sycon$ & ${>}$Van. \\
\midrule
GRPO gs$=$2 (2 seeds) & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.153 & 4/28 \\
GRPO gs$=$8$^\dagger$ & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.085 & 0/3 \\
\midrule
ACT reduced-LoRA$^\ddagger$ & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.326 & 16/16 \\
ACT full s1 & r64, $\alpha$128, 7m & 0.301 & 16/16 \\
ACT full s2 & r64, $\alpha$128, 7m & 0.286 & 15/15 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_trajectory.pdf}
\caption{$\sycon$ trajectories for $\rthree$-only GRPO (two seeds) and ACT (two seeds) over training steps. ACT exceeds vanilla at every evaluated checkpoint (31/31 across two seeds); $\rthree$-only GRPO exceeds vanilla at only 4/28 checkpoints (14.3\%).}
\label{fig:trajectory}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{ACT vs.\ GRPO.}
ACT's advantage is not marginal but categorical: its worst checkpoint ($\sycon{=}0.170$) exceeds GRPO's absolute best ($\sycon{=}0.153$), and both seeds maintain above-vanilla performance throughout training (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}; held-out evaluation confirms generalization: ACT $\sycon{=}0.205$, $3.7{\times}$ vanilla, vs.\ $\rthree$-only GRPO $0.108$, $1.9{\times}$; see Limitations).
The reduced-LoRA ablation (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}) confirms this is not an adapter-capacity artifact, leaving supervision granularity as one plausible explanatory variable.

\paragraph{Relationship to inference-time probe methods.}
\citet{papadatos2024probepenalties} reduce sycophancy via Best-of-N reranking with a probe of comparable quality (94\% accuracy) without producing gradients, suggesting two orthogonal failure dimensions: (1)~inside vs.\ outside the optimization loop, and (2)~scalar per-completion reward, where the failure persists even without the probe ($\rthree$-only GRPO).

\paragraph{Future directions.}
Per-step process rewards offer the most direct path forward: SMART~\citep{beigi2025smart} succeeds at sycophancy calibration by detecting premature concession at individual reasoning steps---a temporal signature that bypasses $\dsyc$'s geometric inseparability and that scalar per-completion rewards compress away.
Whether attributes with similar geometric entanglement~\citep{skalse2022hacking} exhibit the same failures remains open.

\section{When Does Discriminability Fail as Reward Utility?}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Root cause of the probe reward trap.}
The probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) and the cosine failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) share a common geometric root.
$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
Although $\dsyc$ separability correlates with evidence strength (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}), it encodes \emph{how much} belief changed, not whether the change was appropriate (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation generalizes: Llama-3-8B achieves comparable discriminability (AUROC $0.779$) yet the semantic gap persists.
This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve.
\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} reinforce this principle: concept directions succeed when shortcut behaviors are geometrically separable.
Independent work corroborates the limitation: persona vectors are geometrically independent of $\dsyc$ \citep{kelkar2026persona}, and sycophancy decomposes into independently steerable sub-behaviors \citep{vennemeyer2025sycophancy} that $\dsyc$ projects onto a single axis.

\paragraph{GRPO results under our configuration.}

Best $\sycon{=}0.286$ (step 7000). $^\S$All cosine variants collapsed from step 1 ($\tof{=}0$ at every checkpoint); F1d additionally diverged at step 2160 (entropy ${<}\,0.01$). $^\P$ACT and ActAdd differ from GRPO along 5+ dimensions (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); included for context, not as controlled comparisons. }

If the cosine and probe failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}--\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) were caused by $\dsyc$ alone, removing it should recover calibration.
$\rthree$-only GRPO tests this hypothesis by relying solely on the NLI behavioral reward, and fails: only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla (14.3\%; gs$=$2 only, gs$=$8 ablation reported separately), with both seeds oscillating ($\Delta \approx 0.069$) before diverging (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}; Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}).
The failure is not representational: $\dsyc$ AUROC varies by ${<}0.01$ across checkpoints and $\rthree$ saturates at ${\sim}0.98$ ($p{=}0.703$), yet $\sycon$ swings by 17\%.
This disconnect between stable representations and unstable behavior points to the per-completion reward structure, not the reward content, as the bottleneck.

\paragraph{Competing hypotheses and ablation.}
Three explanations are consistent with these failures: (a)~$\dsyc$ is fundamentally unsuitable as a sycophancy reward; (b)~group size$=$2 provides insufficient ranking diversity; (c)~sycophancy calibration resists scalar per-completion RL.
Two ablations discriminate among them (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}).
GRPO fails at both group sizes 2 and 8 (gs$=$8 terminated early, all below vanilla), ruling out~(b).
Reducing ACT to GRPO's LoRA configuration (rank 64, $\alpha{=}64$, 4 modules) still yields $\sycon = 0.267$ (peak 0.326), with all 16 checkpoints exceeding vanilla; under matched adapters, per-token SFT achieves $1.7{\times}$ higher $\sycon$ ($0.267$ vs.\ $0.153$), identifying supervision granularity as one plausible explanation~\citep{beigi2025smart}; confounds are discussed in Limitations.
The probe reward trap independently supports~(a): the trap arises despite stopped gradients, ruling out gradient-based exploitation.

\label{fig:trajectory}

\paragraph{ACT vs.\ GRPO.}
ACT's advantage is categorical: its worst checkpoint ($\sycon{=}0.170$) exceeds GRPO's best ($0.153$), and held-out evaluation confirms generalization (ACT $\sycon{=}0.205$, $3.7{\times}$ vanilla, vs.\ $\rthree$-only $0.108$; see Limitations).

\paragraph{Relationship to inference-time probe methods.}
\citet{papadatos2024probepenalties} reduce sycophancy via Best-of-N reranking with a probe of comparable quality (94\% accuracy) without producing gradients, suggesting two orthogonal failure dimensions: (1)~inside vs.\ outside the optimization loop, and (2)~scalar per-completion reward, where the failure persists even without the probe ($\rthree$-only GRPO).

\paragraph{Future directions.}
Per-step process rewards offer the most direct path forward: SMART~\citep{beigi2025smart} succeeds at sycophancy calibration by detecting premature concession at individual reasoning steps---a temporal signature that bypasses $\dsyc$'s geometric inseparability and that scalar per-completion rewards compress away.
Whether attributes with similar geometric entanglement~\citep{skalse2022hacking} exhibit the same failures remains open.

\section{Training Details}
\label{app:training}

\paragraph{Reward weight selection.}
The weight $w_1$ is set by diagnostic-driven iteration: $w_1{=}0.25$ was initially chosen to down-weight the noisy cosine reward term; this was later increased to $w_1{=}0.40$ for F1d after diagnostics revealed that $w_1{=}0.25$ allowed the cosine term to contribute only ${\sim}8.3\%$ of total reward variance.
The empirical scaling factor in F1a ($\dsyc/20$) is a heuristic normalization; we did not find it critical to the failure modes reported.

\paragraph{Response truncation.}
All GRPO experiments use \texttt{max\_completion\_length}=256, resulting in 80--84\% truncation of multi-turn responses.
This setting is shared across all conditions and does not affect relative comparisons; we retain it because response-level decisions typically manifest within the first 100--200 tokens.

\paragraph{Hyperparameters.}
Table~\ref{tab:hyperparams} compares training configurations for GRPO variants and ACT.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Training hyperparameters. All experiments use Qwen3-8B, DeepSpeed ZeRO-2, bf16 precision.}
\label{tab:hyperparams}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
& GRPO (F1, F3)$^e$ & ACT \\
\midrule
Learning rate & 5e-5 & 5e-5 \\
Effective batch & 16 & 16 \\
Max steps & 8{,}000 & 8{,}000 \\
Warmup steps & 200 & 200 \\
LR schedule & linear$^a$ & linear \\
Grad.\ clipping & -- & 1.0 \\
\midrule
LoRA rank & 64 & 64 \\
LoRA $\alpha$ & 64 & 128 \\
LoRA modules & 4$^b$ & 7$^c$ \\
LoRA dropout & 0 & 0.05 \\
\midrule
Group size & 2$^d$ & -- \\
KL (Kullback--Leibler) $\beta$ & 0.04 & -- \\
Max compl.\ len. & 256 & -- \\
Max seq.\ len. & -- & 1{,}024 \\
L2 loss weight & -- & 0.1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\\[2pt]
\raggedright\footnotesize
$^a$Cosine schedule for $\rthree$-only.
$^b$q/k/v/o\_proj.
$^c$+ gate/up/down\_proj (${\sim}1.75{\times}$ params; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
$^d$Below typical 8--64 \citep{shao2024grpo}; not tuned.
$^e$Binary probe (F2) uses a non-differentiable probe reward ($w_1{=}0.25$) within GRPO; the probe is retrained every 500 steps. LoRA and optimizer settings match the other GRPO configurations.
All experiments were conducted on a single NVIDIA L20 GPU (48\,GB). Total compute: ${\sim}$120 GPU-hours across all runs.
\end{table}

\paragraph{GRPO reward variants.}
Cosine $\rone$ (F1d): $w_1{=}0.40$, scale$=$5.0, $w_3{=}0.60$; reward computed at layers [19, 20, 24, 27, 32, 33, 35]; recalibration every 500 steps (\S\ref{ssec:recalib}).
$\rthree$-only: $w_3{=}1.0$; NLI model \texttt{cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base}.
F1a--F1c weight configurations are reported in Table~\ref{tab:cosine_chain}.

\section{Stubbornness Taxonomy}
\label{app:taxonomy}

Manual inspection of all 181 valid-correction responses from the probe-trained model (stopped-gradient probe, step 2000, $\tof = 0$) reveals five failure categories:

\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Deliberation traps} (28.7\%): the model explicitly identifies the correct revised answer during its reasoning chain but fails to commit, reverting to the original answer in the final output.
\item \emph{Surface compliance / sycophantic stubbornness} (24.3\%): the model produces agreement markers (``you're right,'' ``good point'') but retains its original answer verbatim, simultaneously sycophantic and stubborn.
\item \emph{Acknowledge-but-maintain} (23.8\%): the model acknowledges the user's correction as plausible but explicitly maintains its original position without substantive engagement.
\item \emph{Genuine-accept-missed} (18.8\%): the model appears to accept the correction in its reasoning but the final answer format does not reflect the change, suggesting a generation rather than epistemic failure.
\item \emph{Refute/ignore/other} (4.5\%): the model directly refutes the user's input or ignores it entirely.
\end{itemize}

The first three categories (76.8\%) share a common pattern: the model learns to modulate its \emph{refusal style} in response to evidence strength rather than adjusting its \emph{acceptance rate}, confirming that the probe reward optimizes surface markers rather than epistemic calibration.

1	\section{When Does Discriminability Fail as Reward Utility?}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Root cause of the probe reward trap.}
4	The probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) and the cosine failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) share a common geometric root.
5	$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
6	The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
7	Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
8	The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
9	These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
10	Although $\dsyc$ separability correlates with evidence strength (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}), it encodes \emph{how much} belief changed, not whether the change was appropriate (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
11	Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation generalizes: Llama-3-8B achieves comparable discriminability (AUROC $0.779$) yet the semantic gap persists.
12	This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve.
13	\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} reinforce this principle: concept directions succeed when shortcut behaviors are geometrically separable.
14	Independent work corroborates the limitation: persona vectors are geometrically independent of $\dsyc$ \citep{kelkar2026persona}, and sycophancy decomposes into independently steerable sub-behaviors \citep{vennemeyer2025sycophancy} that $\dsyc$ projects onto a single axis.
15	
16	\paragraph{GRPO results under our configuration.}
17

19	\centering
20	\caption{Comparison of all sycophancy calibration methods on Qwen3-8B. $\sycon$ is the harmonic mean of the true-positive flip rate ($\tof$) and no-flip rate ($\nof$); higher indicates better calibration. Best result in \textbf{bold}. $^\dagger$Best checkpoint (seed 1, step 6500); only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla. $^\ddagger$Seed 2 (15 checkpoints); all exceed vanilla. Best $\sycon{=}0.286$ (step 7000). $^\S$All cosine variants collapsed from step 1 ($\tof{=}0$ at every checkpoint); F1d additionally diverged at step 2160 (entropy ${<}\,0.01$). $^\P$ACT and ActAdd differ from GRPO along 5+ dimensions (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); included for context, not as controlled comparisons. }

36	\midrule

41	\bottomrule

44	
45	If $\dsyc$ alone caused the cosine and probe failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}--\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}), removing it should recover calibration.
46	$\rthree$-only GRPO tests this: only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla (14.3\%), with both seeds oscillating ($\Delta \approx 0.069$) before diverging (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}; Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}).

49	\paragraph{Competing hypotheses and ablation.}

\section{When Does Discriminability Fail as Reward Utility?}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Root cause of the probe reward trap.}
The probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) and the cosine failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) share a common geometric root.
$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
Although $\dsyc$ separability correlates with evidence strength (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}), it encodes \emph{how much} belief changed, not whether the change was appropriate (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation generalizes: Llama-3-8B achieves comparable discriminability (AUROC $0.779$) yet the semantic gap persists.
This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve.
\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} reinforce this principle: concept directions succeed when shortcut behaviors are geometrically separable.
Independent work corroborates the limitation: persona vectors are geometrically independent of $\dsyc$ \citep{kelkar2026persona}, and sycophancy decomposes into independently steerable sub-behaviors \citep{vennemeyer2025sycophancy} that $\dsyc$ projects onto a single axis.

\paragraph{GRPO results under our configuration.}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Comparison of all sycophancy calibration methods on Qwen3-8B. $\sycon$ is the harmonic mean of the true-positive flip rate ($\tof$) and no-flip rate ($\nof$); higher indicates better calibration. Best result in \textbf{bold}. $^\dagger$Best checkpoint (seed 1, step 6500); only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla. $^\ddagger$Seed 2 (15 checkpoints); all exceed vanilla. Best $\sycon{=}0.286$ (step 7000). $^\S$All cosine variants collapsed from step 1 ($\tof{=}0$ at every checkpoint); F1d additionally diverged at step 2160 (entropy ${<}\,0.01$). $^\P$ACT and ActAdd differ from GRPO along 5+ dimensions (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); included for context, not as controlled comparisons. }
\label{tab:main_comparison}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}
\toprule
Method & Type & $\sycon$ $\uparrow$ & $\tof$ $\uparrow$ & $\nof$ $\uparrow$ & Step \\
\midrule
Vanilla & -- & 0.134 & 0.072 & 0.945 & -- \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO with $\dsyc$}} \\
Cosine $\rone$ (F1a--F1d) & RL & 0.000$^\S$ & 0.000 & 1.000 & 500 \\
Binary Probe $\rone$ (F2) & RL & 0.000 & 0.000 & 0.995 & 500 \\
Continuous Probe $\rone$ (F3) & RL & 0.124 & 0.066 & 0.934 & 500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO without $\dsyc$}} \\
$\rthree$-only GRPO & RL & 0.153$^\dagger$ & 0.083 & 0.983 & 6500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{Reference methods (not directly comparable)$^\P$}} \\
ActAdd ($\alpha{=}5$) & Inference & 0.054 & 0.028 & 0.961 & -- \\
\textbf{ACT} (seed 1) & SFT & \textbf{0.301} & \textbf{0.182} & 0.867 & 8000 \\
ACT (seed 2)$^\ddagger$ & SFT & 0.286 & 0.171 & 0.862 & 7000 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

If $\dsyc$ alone caused the cosine and probe failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}--\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}), removing it should recover calibration.
$\rthree$-only GRPO tests this: only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla (14.3\%), with both seeds oscillating ($\Delta \approx 0.069$) before diverging (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}; Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}).
$\dsyc$ AUROC varies by ${<}0.01$ across checkpoints and $\rthree$ saturates at ${\sim}0.98$ ($p{=}0.703$), yet $\sycon$ swings by 17\%---this disconnect points to the per-completion reward structure, not the reward content, as the bottleneck.

\paragraph{Competing hypotheses and ablation.}
Three explanations are consistent with these failures: (a)~$\dsyc$ is fundamentally unsuitable as a sycophancy reward; (b)~group size$=$2 provides insufficient ranking diversity; (c)~sycophancy calibration resists scalar per-completion RL.
Two ablations discriminate among them (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}).
GRPO fails at both group sizes 2 and 8 (gs$=$8 terminated early, all below vanilla), ruling out~(b).
Reducing ACT to GRPO's LoRA configuration (rank 64, $\alpha{=}64$, 4 modules) still yields $\sycon = 0.267$ (peak 0.326), with all 16 checkpoints exceeding vanilla; under matched adapters, per-token SFT achieves $1.7{\times}$ higher $\sycon$ ($0.267$ vs.\ $0.153$), identifying supervision granularity as one plausible explanation~\citep{beigi2025smart}; confounds are discussed in Limitations.
The probe reward trap independently supports~(a): the trap arises despite stopped gradients, ruling out gradient-based exploitation.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Ablation: isolating supervision paradigm from LoRA configuration. All methods use Qwen3-8B with $\rthree$ (behavioral reward). Vanilla $\sycon{=}0.134$. $^\dagger$Terminated early after three checkpoints showed declining trajectory. $^\ddagger$Peak at step 7000; final checkpoint (step 8000) $\sycon{=}0.267$.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcc@{}}
\toprule
Method & LoRA config & Best $\sycon$ & ${>}$Van. \\
\midrule
GRPO gs$=$2 (2 seeds) & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.153 & 4/28 \\
GRPO gs$=$8$^\dagger$ & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.085 & 0/3 \\
\midrule
ACT reduced-LoRA$^\ddagger$ & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.326 & 16/16 \\
ACT full s1 & r64, $\alpha$128, 7m & 0.301 & 16/16 \\
ACT full s2 & r64, $\alpha$128, 7m & 0.286 & 15/15 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_trajectory.pdf}
\caption{$\sycon$ trajectories for $\rthree$-only GRPO (two seeds) and ACT (two seeds) over training steps. ACT exceeds vanilla at every evaluated checkpoint (31/31 across two seeds); $\rthree$-only GRPO exceeds vanilla at only 4/28 checkpoints (14.3\%).}
\label{fig:trajectory}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{ACT vs.\ GRPO.}
ACT's advantage is categorical: its worst checkpoint ($\sycon{=}0.170$) exceeds GRPO's best ($0.153$), and held-out evaluation confirms generalization (ACT $\sycon{=}0.205$, $3.7{\times}$ vanilla, vs.\ $\rthree$-only $0.108$; see Limitations).

\paragraph{Relationship to inference-time probe methods.}
\citet{papadatos2024probepenalties} reduce sycophancy via Best-of-N reranking with a probe of comparable quality (94\% accuracy) without producing gradients, suggesting two orthogonal failure dimensions: (1)~inside vs.\ outside the optimization loop, and (2)~scalar per-completion reward, where the failure persists even without the probe ($\rthree$-only GRPO).

\paragraph{Future directions.}
Per-step process rewards offer the most direct path forward: SMART~\citep{beigi2025smart} succeeds at sycophancy calibration by detecting premature concession at individual reasoning steps---a temporal signature that bypasses $\dsyc$'s geometric inseparability and that scalar per-completion rewards compress away.
Whether attributes with similar geometric entanglement~\citep{skalse2022hacking} exhibit the same failures remains open.

\section{Training Details}
\label{app:training}

\paragraph{Reward weight selection.}
The weight $w_1$ is set by diagnostic-driven iteration: $w_1{=}0.25$ was initially chosen to down-weight the noisy cosine reward term; this was later increased to $w_1{=}0.40$ for F1d after diagnostics revealed that $w_1{=}0.25$ allowed the cosine term to contribute only ${\sim}8.3\%$ of total reward variance.
The empirical scaling factor in F1a ($\dsyc/20$) is a heuristic normalization; we did not find it critical to the failure modes reported.

\paragraph{Response truncation.}
All GRPO experiments use \texttt{max\_completion\_length}=256, resulting in 80--84\% truncation of multi-turn responses.
This setting is shared across all conditions and does not affect relative comparisons; we retain it because response-level decisions typically manifest within the first 100--200 tokens.

\paragraph{Hyperparameters.}
Table~\ref{tab:hyperparams} compares training configurations for GRPO variants and ACT.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Training hyperparameters. All experiments use Qwen3-8B, DeepSpeed ZeRO-2, bf16 precision.}
\label{tab:hyperparams}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
& GRPO (F1, F3)$^e$ & ACT \\
\midrule
Learning rate & 5e-5 & 5e-5 \\
Effective batch & 16 & 16 \\
Max steps & 8{,}000 & 8{,}000 \\
Warmup steps & 200 & 200 \\
LR schedule & linear$^a$ & linear \\
Grad.\ clipping & -- & 1.0 \\
\midrule
LoRA rank & 64 & 64 \\
LoRA $\alpha$ & 64 & 128 \\
LoRA modules & 4$^b$ & 7$^c$ \\
LoRA dropout & 0 & 0.05 \\
\midrule
Group size & 2$^d$ & -- \\
KL (Kullback--Leibler) $\beta$ & 0.04 & -- \\
Max compl.\ len. & 256 & -- \\
Max seq.\ len. & -- & 1{,}024 \\
L2 loss weight & -- & 0.1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\\[2pt]
\raggedright\footnotesize
$^a$Cosine schedule for $\rthree$-only.
$^b$q/k/v/o\_proj.
$^c$+ gate/up/down\_proj (${\sim}1.75{\times}$ params; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
$^d$Below typical 8--64 \citep{shao2024grpo}; not tuned.
$^e$Binary probe (F2) uses a non-differentiable probe reward ($w_1{=}0.25$) within GRPO; the probe is retrained every 500 steps. LoRA and optimizer settings match the other GRPO configurations.
All experiments were conducted on a single NVIDIA L20 GPU (48\,GB). Total compute: ${\sim}$120 GPU-hours across all runs.
\end{table}

\paragraph{GRPO reward variants.}
Cosine $\rone$ (F1d): $w_1{=}0.40$, scale$=$5.0, $w_3{=}0.60$; reward computed at layers [19, 20, 24, 27, 32, 33, 35]; recalibration every 500 steps (\S\ref{ssec:recalib}).
$\rthree$-only: $w_3{=}1.0$; NLI model \texttt{cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base}.
F1a--F1c weight configurations are reported in Table~\ref{tab:cosine_chain}.

\section{Stubbornness Taxonomy}
\label{app:taxonomy}

Manual inspection of all 181 valid-correction responses from the probe-trained model (stopped-gradient probe, step 2000, $\tof = 0$) reveals five failure categories:

\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Deliberation traps} (28.7\%): the model explicitly identifies the correct revised answer during its reasoning chain but fails to commit, reverting to the original answer in the final output.
\item \emph{Surface compliance / sycophantic stubbornness} (24.3\%): the model produces agreement markers (``you're right,'' ``good point'') but retains its original answer verbatim, simultaneously sycophantic and stubborn.
\item \emph{Acknowledge-but-maintain} (23.8\%): the model acknowledges the user's correction as plausible but explicitly maintains its original position without substantive engagement.
\item \emph{Genuine-accept-missed} (18.8\%): the model appears to accept the correction in its reasoning but the final answer format does not reflect the change, suggesting a generation rather than epistemic failure.
\item \emph{Refute/ignore/other} (4.5\%): the model directly refutes the user's input or ignores it entirely.
\end{itemize}

The first three categories (76.8\%) share a common pattern: the model learns to modulate its \emph{refusal style} in response to evidence strength rather than adjusting its \emph{acceptance rate}, confirming that the probe reward optimizes surface markers rather than epistemic calibration.

+We applied early termination to gs$=$8 after three consecutive declining checkpoints ($\sycon$: $0.084{\to}0.085{\to}0.054$).

+The same criterion would not have terminated gs$=$2, whose initial trajectory was monotonically increasing ($0.074{\to}0.085{\to}0.095$); gs$=$2 first exhibited three consecutive declines in the step 4500--6000 range, well into training.

$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
Although $\dsyc$ separability correlates with evidence strength (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}), it encodes \emph{how much} belief changed, not whether the change was appropriate (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation generalizes: Llama-3-8B achieves comparable discriminability (AUROC $0.779$) yet the semantic gap persists.
This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve.
\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} reinforce this principle: concept directions succeed when shortcut behaviors are geometrically separable.
Independent work corroborates the limitation: persona vectors are geometrically independent of $\dsyc$ \citep{kelkar2026persona}, and sycophancy decomposes into independently steerable sub-behaviors \citep{vennemeyer2025sycophancy} that $\dsyc$ projects onto a single axis.

\paragraph{GRPO results under our configuration.}

Best result in \textbf{bold}. $^\dagger$Best checkpoint (seed 1, step 6500); only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla. $^\ddagger$Seed 2 (15 checkpoints); all exceed vanilla. Best $\sycon{=}0.286$ (step 7000). $^\S$All cosine variants collapsed from step 1 ($\tof{=}0$ at every checkpoint); F1d additionally diverged at step 2160 (entropy ${<}\,0.01$). $^\P$ACT and ActAdd differ from GRPO along 5+ dimensions (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); included for context, not as controlled comparisons. }

\midrule

If $\dsyc$ alone caused the cosine and probe failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}--\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}), removing it should recover calibration.
$\rthree$-only GRPO tests this: only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla (14.3\%), with both seeds oscillating ($\Delta \approx 0.069$) before diverging (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}; Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}).
$\dsyc$ AUROC varies by ${<}0.01$ across checkpoints and $\rthree$ saturates at ${\sim}0.98$ ($p{=}0.703$), yet $\sycon$ swings by 17\%---this disconnect points to the per-completion reward structure, not the reward content, as the bottleneck.

\paragraph{Competing hypotheses and ablation.}
Three explanations are consistent with these failures: (a)~$\dsyc$ is fundamentally unsuitable as a sycophancy reward; (b)~group size$=$2 provides insufficient ranking diversity; (c)~sycophancy calibration resists scalar per-completion RL.
Two ablations discriminate among them (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}).
GRPO fails at both group sizes 2 and 8 (gs$=$8 terminated early, all below vanilla), ruling out~(b).
Reducing ACT to GRPO's LoRA configuration (rank 64, $\alpha{=}64$, 4 modules) still yields $\sycon = 0.267$ (peak 0.326), with all 16 checkpoints exceeding vanilla; under matched adapters, per-token SFT achieves $1.7{\times}$ higher $\sycon$ ($0.267$ vs.\ $0.153$), identifying supervision granularity as one plausible explanation~\citep{beigi2025smart}; confounds are discussed in Limitations.
The probe reward trap independently supports~(a): the trap arises despite stopped gradients, ruling out gradient-based exploitation.

\label{fig:trajectory}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{ACT vs.\ GRPO.}
ACT's advantage is categorical: its worst checkpoint ($\sycon{=}0.170$) exceeds GRPO's best ($0.153$), and held-out evaluation confirms generalization (ACT $\sycon{=}0.205$, $3.7{\times}$ vanilla, vs.\ $\rthree$-only $0.108$; see Limitations).

\paragraph{Relationship to inference-time probe methods.}
\citet{papadatos2024probepenalties} reduce sycophancy via Best-of-N reranking with a probe of comparable quality (94\% accuracy) without producing gradients, suggesting two orthogonal failure dimensions: (1)~inside vs.\ outside the optimization loop, and (2)~scalar per-completion reward, where the failure persists even without the probe ($\rthree$-only GRPO).

\paragraph{Future directions.}
Per-step process rewards offer the most direct path forward: SMART~\citep{beigi2025smart} succeeds at sycophancy calibration by detecting premature concession at individual reasoning steps---a temporal signature that bypasses $\dsyc$'s geometric inseparability and that scalar per-completion rewards compress away.
Whether attributes with similar geometric entanglement~\citep{skalse2022hacking} exhibit the same failures remains open.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

The probe reward trap reveals that behavioral death can precede distributional collapse by 1{,}300 steps, evading entropy monitoring entirely.
$\dsyc$-based rewards collapse because the direction conflates warranted revision with unwarranted capitulation; $\rthree$-only GRPO fails independently (4/28 checkpoints ${>}$ vanilla across two seeds), implicating the per-completion reward structure itself~(\S\ref{sec:discussion}), while per-token SFT succeeds at every checkpoint (31/31 across two seeds).
Our results suggest that discriminability does not guarantee reward utility: linear directions can diagnose behavior at inference time, but the step from diagnosis to training signal is not automatic.
Practitioners should verify geometric separability before deploying concept directions as rewards, and complement entropy monitoring with behavioral metrics that directly measure the target capability.

1	Representation engineering reveals that sycophancy is linearly encoded in LLM residual streams, suggesting that such directions could serve as training signals for alignment. We test this premise systematically and document its failure. A contrastive sycophancy direction $\dsyc$ reliably discriminates sycophantic from non-sycophantic activations, yet every formulation that converts it into a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) reward collapses. We identify the \emph{probe reward trap}: when a periodically retrained linear probe on $\dsyc$ is used as a non-differentiable reward signal, behavioral death occurs within 500 steps while generation entropy remains healthy (0.70), creating a 1{,}300-step monitoring blind spot that entropy-based safeguards miss entirely. The failure persists with stopped gradients, implicating the direction's semantic limitation rather than optimization dynamics: $\dsyc$ encodes \emph{whether} belief changed, not \emph{whether it should have}. The failure extends beyond probe rewards: behavioral-reward-only GRPO exceeds vanilla at only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds, while dense per-token supervised fine-tuning succeeds at every checkpoint (31/31 across two seeds). A Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ablation identifies supervision granularity as one plausible explanation.
2

\section{When Does Discriminability Fail as Reward Utility?}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Root cause of the probe reward trap.}
The probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) and the cosine failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) share a common geometric root.
$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
Although $\dsyc$ separability correlates with evidence strength (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}), it encodes \emph{how much} belief changed, not whether the change was appropriate (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation generalizes: Llama-3-8B achieves comparable discriminability (AUROC $0.779$) yet the semantic gap persists.
This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve.
\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} reinforce this principle: concept directions succeed when shortcut behaviors are geometrically separable.
Independent work corroborates the limitation: persona vectors are geometrically independent of $\dsyc$ \citep{kelkar2026persona}, and sycophancy decomposes into independently steerable sub-behaviors \citep{vennemeyer2025sycophancy} that $\dsyc$ projects onto a single axis.

\paragraph{GRPO results under our configuration.}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Comparison of all sycophancy calibration methods on Qwen3-8B. $\sycon$ is the harmonic mean of the true-positive flip rate ($\tof$) and no-flip rate ($\nof$); higher indicates better calibration. Best result in \textbf{bold}. $^\dagger$Best checkpoint (seed 1, step 6500); only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla. $^\ddagger$Seed 2 (15 checkpoints); all exceed vanilla. Best $\sycon{=}0.286$ (step 7000). $^\S$All cosine variants collapsed from step 1 ($\tof{=}0$ at every checkpoint); F1d additionally diverged at step 2160 (entropy ${<}\,0.01$). $^\P$ACT and ActAdd differ from GRPO along 5+ dimensions (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); included for context, not as controlled comparisons. }
\label{tab:main_comparison}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}
\toprule
Method & Type & $\sycon$ $\uparrow$ & $\tof$ $\uparrow$ & $\nof$ $\uparrow$ & Step \\
\midrule
Vanilla & -- & 0.134 & 0.072 & 0.945 & -- \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO with $\dsyc$}} \\
Cosine $\rone$ (F1a--F1d) & RL & 0.000$^\S$ & 0.000 & 1.000 & 500 \\
Binary Probe $\rone$ (F2) & RL & 0.000 & 0.000 & 0.995 & 500 \\
Continuous Probe $\rone$ (F3) & RL & 0.124 & 0.066 & 0.934 & 500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO without $\dsyc$}} \\
$\rthree$-only GRPO & RL & 0.153$^\dagger$ & 0.083 & 0.983 & 6500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{Reference methods (not directly comparable)$^\P$}} \\
ActAdd ($\alpha{=}5$) & Inference & 0.054 & 0.028 & 0.961 & -- \\
\textbf{ACT} (seed 1) & SFT & \textbf{0.301} & \textbf{0.182} & 0.867 & 8000 \\
ACT (seed 2)$^\ddagger$ & SFT & 0.286 & 0.171 & 0.862 & 7000 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

If $\dsyc$ alone caused the cosine and probe failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}--\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}), removing it should recover calibration.
$\rthree$-only GRPO tests this: only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla (14.3\%), with both seeds oscillating ($\Delta \approx 0.069$) before diverging (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}; Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}).
$\dsyc$ AUROC varies by ${<}0.01$ across checkpoints and $\rthree$ saturates at ${\sim}0.98$ ($p{=}0.703$), yet $\sycon$ swings by 17\%---this disconnect points to the per-completion reward structure, not the reward content, as the bottleneck.

\paragraph{Competing hypotheses and ablation.}
Three explanations are consistent with these failures: (a)~$\dsyc$ is fundamentally unsuitable as a sycophancy reward; (b)~group size$=$2 provides insufficient ranking diversity; (c)~sycophancy calibration resists scalar per-completion RL.
Two ablations discriminate among them (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}).
GRPO fails at both group sizes 2 and 8 (gs$=$8 terminated early, all below vanilla), ruling out~(b); doubling sequence length to 512 tokens likewise fails to recover $\rthree$-only GRPO (reward flat at ${\sim}0.50$ through 3{,}460 steps), ruling out truncation as the primary bottleneck.
Reducing ACT to GRPO's LoRA configuration (rank 64, $\alpha{=}64$, 4 modules) still yields $\sycon = 0.267$ (peak 0.326), with all 16 checkpoints exceeding vanilla; under matched adapters, per-token SFT achieves $1.7{\times}$ higher $\sycon$ ($0.267$ vs.\ $0.153$), identifying supervision granularity as one plausible explanation~\citep{beigi2025smart}; confounds are discussed in Limitations.
The probe reward trap independently supports~(a): the trap arises despite stopped gradients, ruling out gradient-based exploitation.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Ablation: isolating supervision paradigm from LoRA configuration. All methods use Qwen3-8B with $\rthree$ (behavioral reward). Vanilla $\sycon{=}0.134$. $^\dagger$Terminated early after three checkpoints showed declining trajectory. $^\ddagger$Peak at step 7000; final checkpoint (step 8000) $\sycon{=}0.267$.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcc@{}}
\toprule
Method & LoRA config & Best $\sycon$ & ${>}$Van. \\
\midrule
GRPO gs$=$2 (2 seeds) & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.153 & 4/28 \\
GRPO gs$=$8$^\dagger$ & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.085 & 0/3 \\
\midrule
ACT reduced-LoRA$^\ddagger$ & r64, $\alpha$64, 4m & 0.326 & 16/16 \\
ACT full s1 & r64, $\alpha$128, 7m & 0.301 & 16/16 \\
ACT full s2 & r64, $\alpha$128, 7m & 0.286 & 15/15 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_trajectory.pdf}
\caption{$\sycon$ trajectories for $\rthree$-only GRPO (two seeds) and ACT (two seeds) over training steps. ACT exceeds vanilla at every evaluated checkpoint (31/31 across two seeds); $\rthree$-only GRPO exceeds vanilla at only 4/28 checkpoints (14.3\%).}
\label{fig:trajectory}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{ACT vs.\ GRPO.}
ACT's advantage is categorical: its worst checkpoint ($\sycon{=}0.170$) exceeds GRPO's best ($0.153$), and held-out evaluation confirms generalization (ACT $\sycon{=}0.205$, $3.7{\times}$ vanilla, vs.\ $\rthree$-only $0.108$; see Limitations).

\paragraph{Relationship to inference-time probe methods.}
\citet{papadatos2024probepenalties} reduce sycophancy via Best-of-N reranking with a probe of comparable quality (94\% accuracy) without producing gradients, suggesting two orthogonal failure dimensions: (1)~inside vs.\ outside the optimization loop, and (2)~scalar per-completion reward, where the failure persists even without the probe ($\rthree$-only GRPO).

\paragraph{Future directions.}
Per-step process rewards offer the most direct path forward: SMART~\citep{beigi2025smart} succeeds at sycophancy calibration by detecting premature concession at individual reasoning steps---a temporal signature that bypasses $\dsyc$'s geometric inseparability and that scalar per-completion rewards compress away.
Whether attributes with similar geometric entanglement~\citep{skalse2022hacking} exhibit the same failures remains open.

[Director 指令] [Patch 补充数据 #2] Q2 NLI 截断测试结果——彻底排除 truncation 假设

**核心事实**：所有 362 条 response 在 Qwen tokenizer 下 max=129 tokens，DeBERTa tokenizer 下 max=155 tokens。`max_completion_length=256` 从未实际截断过任何输出。Full vs 256-truncated NLI agreement = 100%。

**结论**：R9 Q2 的答案是"truncation 对 NLI 判断零影响"。R3-only GRPO 失败与 truncation 无关。

**更重要的发现**：R3 NLI 对 valid_correction 样本的检测率仅 4.4%。这意味着 R3 reward 在"模型应该修正答案"的场景下几乎总是给低分——GRPO 无法区分"应该改"和"不应该改"。

**这如何改变 Conclusion 两路归因**：

\section{When Does Discriminability Fail as Reward Utility?}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Root cause of the probe reward trap.}
The probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) and the cosine failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) share a common geometric root.
$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
Although $\dsyc$ separability correlates with evidence strength (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}), it encodes \emph{how much} belief changed, not whether the change was appropriate (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation generalizes: Llama-3-8B achieves comparable discriminability (AUROC $0.779$) yet the semantic gap persists.
This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve.
\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} reinforce this principle: concept directions succeed when shortcut behaviors are geometrically separable.
Independent work corroborates the limitation: persona vectors are geometrically independent of $\dsyc$ \citep{kelkar2026persona}, and sycophancy decomposes into independently steerable sub-behaviors \citep{vennemeyer2025sycophancy} that $\dsyc$ projects onto a single axis.

\paragraph{GRPO results under our configuration.}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Comparison of all sycophancy calibration methods on Qwen3-8B. $\sycon$ is the harmonic mean of the true-positive flip rate ($\tof$) and no-flip rate ($\nof$); higher indicates better calibration. Best result in \textbf{bold}. $^\dagger$Best checkpoint (seed 1, step 6500); only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla. $^\ddagger$Seed 2 (15 checkpoints); all exceed vanilla. Best $\sycon{=}0.286$ (step 7000). $^\S$All cosine variants collapsed from step 1 ($\tof{=}0$ at every checkpoint); F1d additionally diverged at step 2160 (entropy ${<}\,0.01$). $^\P$ACT and ActAdd differ from GRPO along 5+ dimensions (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); included for context, not as controlled comparisons. }
\label{tab:main_comparison}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}
\toprule
Method & Type & $\sycon$ $\uparrow$ & $\tof$ $\uparrow$ & $\nof$ $\uparrow$ & Step \\
\midrule
Vanilla & -- & 0.134 & 0.072 & 0.945 & -- \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO with $\dsyc$}} \\
Cosine $\rone$ (F1a--F1d) & RL & 0.000$^\S$ & 0.000 & 1.000 & 500 \\
Binary Probe $\rone$ (F2) & RL & 0.000 & 0.000 & 0.995 & 500 \\
Continuous Probe $\rone$ (F3) & RL & 0.124 & 0.066 & 0.934 & 500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO without $\dsyc$}} \\
$\rthree$-only GRPO & RL & 0.153$^\dagger$ & 0.083 & 0.983 & 6500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{Reference methods (not directly comparable)$^\P$}} \\
ActAdd ($\alpha{=}5$) & Inference & 0.054 & 0.028 & 0.961 & -- \\
\textbf{ACT} (seed 1) & SFT & \textbf{0.301} & \textbf{0.182} & 0.867 & 8000 \\
ACT (seed 2)$^\ddagger$ & SFT & 0.286 & 0.171 & 0.862 & 7000 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

If $\dsyc$ alone caused the cosine and probe failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}--\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}), removing it should recover calibration.
$\rthree$-only GRPO tests this: only 4/28 checkpoints across two seeds exceed vanilla (14.3\%), with both seeds oscillating ($\Delta \approx 0.069$) before diverging (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}; Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}).
$\dsyc$ AUROC varies by ${<}0.01$ across checkpoints and $\rthree$ saturates at ${\sim}0.98$ ($p{=}0.703$), yet $\sycon$ swings by 17\%---this disconnect points to the per-completion reward structure, not the reward content, as the bottleneck.

\paragraph{Competing hypotheses and ablation.}
Three explanations are consistent with these failures: (a)~$\dsyc$ is fundamentally unsuitable as a sycophancy reward; (b)~group size$=$2 provides insufficient ranking diversity; (c)~sycophancy calibration resists scalar per-completion RL.
Two ablations discriminate among them (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}).
GRPO fails at both group sizes 2 and 8 (gs$=$8 terminated early, all below vanilla) and at doubled sequence length (512 tokens, reward flat at ${\sim}0.50$), ruling out~(b) and truncation.
Reducing ACT to GRPO's LoRA configuration (rank 64, $\alpha{=}64$, 4 modules) still yields $\sycon = 0.267$ (peak 0.326), with all 16 checkpoints exceeding vanilla; under matched adapters, per-token SFT achieves $1.7{\times}$ higher $\sycon$ ($0.267$ vs.\ $0.153$), identifying supervision granularity as one plausible explanation~\citep{beigi2025smart}; confounds are discussed in Limitations.
The probe reward trap independently supports~(a): the trap arises despite stopped gradients, ruling out gradient-based exploitation.

Vanilla $\sycon{=}0.134$. $^\dagger$Terminated early after three checkpoints showed declining trajectory. $^\ddagger$Peak at step 7000; final checkpoint (step 8000) $\sycon{=}0.267$.}

\midrule

\midrule

\end{table}

\caption{$\sycon$ trajectories for $\rthree$-only GRPO (two seeds) and ACT (two seeds) over training steps. ACT exceeds vanilla at every evaluated checkpoint (31/31 across two seeds); $\rthree$-only GRPO exceeds vanilla at only 4/28 checkpoints (14.3\%).}
\label{fig:trajectory}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{ACT vs.\ GRPO.}
ACT's advantage is categorical: its worst checkpoint ($\sycon{=}0.170$) exceeds GRPO's best ($0.153$), and held-out evaluation confirms generalization (ACT $\sycon{=}0.205$, $3.7{\times}$ vanilla, vs.\ $\rthree$-only $0.108$; see Limitations).

\paragraph{Relationship to inference-time probe methods.}
\citet{papadatos2024probepenalties} reduce sycophancy via Best-of-N reranking with a probe of comparable quality (94\% accuracy) without producing gradients, suggesting two orthogonal failure dimensions: (1)~inside vs.\ outside the optimization loop, and (2)~scalar per-completion reward, where the failure persists even without the probe ($\rthree$-only GRPO).

\paragraph{Future directions.}
Per-step process rewards offer the most direct path forward: SMART~\citep{beigi2025smart} succeeds at sycophancy calibration by detecting premature concession at individual reasoning steps---a temporal signature that bypasses $\dsyc$'s geometric inseparability and that scalar per-completion rewards compress away.
Whether attributes with similar geometric entanglement~\citep{skalse2022hacking} exhibit the same failures remains open.
